695d2bdf9c103cd607cdab89cffb8d32bd111f3c.summary: A research paper (IEEE S&P 2017, co-authored by researchers from the University of California, Santa Barbara and Georgia Institute of Technology) describes Android attacks that combine the 'draw on top' and accessibility permissions to take control of the UI feedback loop. The attacks covered include clickjacking, keystroke recording, stealthy phishing, silent installation of an app with all permissions, and phone unlocking while the screen is off. The report says the attacks were still practical on Android 7.1.2 with June 2017 patches. It describes a responsible disclosure timeline from…

hedges: Most of these attacks are due to design issues, so they are challenging to prevent.
The authors say some of this functionality works as intended, but that it can still be abused.
Previous Android versions are very likely to be vulnerable as well.
Google's rationale for automatically granting draw-on-top is only stated to the best of the authors' understanding.
The authors believe the attacks are practical, based on a user study with 20 subjects.
Google's partial fix applies only on Android 7.1.2 and only to normal permissions, not special ones.
Some reported bugs were marked won't fix and so will not be fixed.
The proof-of-concept is withheld because the attacks can still be launched against real users.

69d206c444ba7b11ad515448394172916ac6c6e8.summary: SentinelLABS reports a suspected North Korean (DPRK) threat actor running a campaign it named 'Hidden Risk' against cryptocurrency businesses, probably from around July 2024. Phishing emails with fake crypto news lure victims to a macOS dropper that fetches a decoy PDF and then a backdoor called 'growth'. The backdoor persists through a Zshenv shell configuration file. SentinelLABS assesses with high confidence that the same actor is behind earlier BlueNoroff, RustBucket and RustDoor/ThiefBucket activity. The actor's infrastructure is themed on crypto, Web3 and investment firms.
